opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for me it's very much an assistant and not a replacement. I still like to be the one driving. Most of my work is either writing educational code, like for my books, or research prototyping, and in both cases I really need to understand every line. If I just let a model generate a whole implementation, I'd end up spending more time reading and verifying it than I would have spent writing it myself.

So where it really shines for me is the tedious stuff. Things like writing a quick plotting function, remembering the exact arguments for some matplotlib call, converting a script into a command-line tool with argparse, or writing boilerplate for unit tests. That's where I'm happy to hand things off, because it's easy to check and there isn't much creative decision-making involved.

I also use it a lot as a sort of second pair of eyes. When I've written something, say a from-scratch implementation of an attention mechanism, I'll paste it in and ask, "Do you see any bugs or inefficiencies here?" Sometimes it catches small things, like a shape issue or a missing detail, and sometimes it suggests things that are wrong. Either way, it's a good prompt for me to think more carefully about the code.

What I'm a bit more cautious about is the fully agentic workflow, where the model goes off, edits ten files, and comes back. That can be great for certain tasks, but I find I lose the mental model of my own codebase. And for me, especially when teaching, that mental model is kind of the whole point.

So in short, I'd say I like it as a very knowledgeable pair programmer that I consult, rather than something I delegate entire projects to. It's a productivity boost, but I still want to stay in the loop.

r001.rationale: The speaker says they use the assistant as a “second pair of eyes” by sharing code they wrote and asking it to spot bugs or inefficiencies.

r002.rationale: The response notes that suggestions can be wrong, but does not say to experimentally verify whether suggested optimizations make code faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and I think my answer has actually shifted a bit over the last couple of years. I'd say I use LLM assistants in two pretty distinct modes, and I try to be deliberate about keeping them separate.

The first mode is what I'd call the "I know exactly what I want, just type it for me" mode. So things like writing boilerplate, converting a function from one framework to another, writing a quick plotting function, generating a test case for something I already understand. There the LLM is basically a fast autocomplete, and it's great. It saves me a lot of time, and honestly it's made me more willing to write the small utility scripts I used to be too lazy to write.

The second mode is more like having a conversation with a colleague. If I'm implementing something from a paper, say a new attention variant or a different positional encoding, I'll sometimes describe what I'm trying to do and ask it to sanity-check my reasoning or point out edge cases I might be missing. I find that useful, but I'm much more careful there, because the failure mode is subtle. The code will look right, it'll run, and it'll be wrong in a way you only catch if you actually understand the thing.

And that's really my main principle: I don't let it write code I couldn't have written myself. For the kind of work I do, which is a lot of educational material and implementing things from scratch, the whole point is understanding. If I just accept a generated implementation of, say, a KV cache, and I didn't work through it, then I've lost the thing that was valuable about doing it in the first place. So for anything that's core to what I'm trying to learn or teach, I'll write it myself first and then maybe use the model to review it or compare approaches.

The other thing I'd mention is that I keep it out of the loop when I'm thinking. Early on I noticed that if I reached for the assistant too quickly, I'd stop forming my own mental model of the problem. So now I'll often sketch the structure on my own, decide how I want things organized, and only then bring the model in for the parts that are mechanical.

So in short: great for the mechanical stuff, useful as a reviewer or a rubber duck, but I try to stay in the driver's seat for anything where understanding is the actual goal.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they write core code themselves and then use the model to review it or compare approaches, describing it as a reviewer or rubber duck.

astra-6.text:
I like it to be a collaborator, where I’m still driving the process. Usually, I want to think through the problem first, figure out the structure, and then ask the assistant to help with a specific piece. That might be writing some boilerplate, suggesting a test, or helping me understand an error.

The important part for me is that I can review and understand what it produces. If I get a huge block of code that looks plausible but I don’t really follow, that can create more work later. So I prefer smaller iterations: make a change, check it, and then move on. It’s useful when it helps me keep momentum without losing my understanding of the code.

sol-6.1.text: I like to keep it interactive. Usually, I have an idea of what I want to build, and I use the assistant to help with a particular piece—writing a function, explaining an error, or suggesting a different approach. Then I look at the code, run it, and iterate. The important thing for me is that I can still follow what’s happening. If it produces a big chunk of code that I don’t understand, reviewing it can become more work than writing it myself. So I prefer small steps, with me staying involved in the decisions.
